SAS (Statistical Analysis System) is a comprehensive software suite for advanced data analysis, business intelligence, data management, and predictive analytics.

1.17 General SAS statement rules



All SAS statements (except lines of data) must end with a semicolon.
SAS statements begin with a SAS keyword, such as TITLE, DATA, INPUT, DATALINES, RUN, PROC, and VAR.
SAS statements are not case-sensitive. You can type code in all caps, all lowercase, or a mix of both.
Words in SAS statements are separated by blanks or special characters (such as =, +, or *).

2.4 The LIBNAME statement
libname libref "path-to-folder";

libref is the short name you will use for the library (up to 8 characters, starting with a letter or underscore).
The path is the folder that holds your data, not a single file.
After this runs, refer to any table in that folder as libref.table-name.

proc contents data=ma505.overwatch;

A libref is:

a pointer, or shortcut, to existing data
the libref may be deleted, but the data stays in the same place
to get the libref back, run the LIBNAME statement again

2.8 The Libraries pane
In SAS Studio, open Libraries in the navigation pane, then My Libraries.


WORK: tables you created without a libref, like example. These disappear when you sign out.
SASHELP: sample datasets. Double-click CLASS to view the sashelp.class table.
MA505: appears after you run your LIBNAME statement. Click Refresh if you don’t see it.

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.9 Libraries last for one session

The libref is temporary: SAS forgets it when your session ends. The data is permanent: your tables stay in the folder. Run LIBNAME again (or put it in your autoexec) to reconnect.


So why use libraries?

Short names instead of long paths: ma505.overwatch instead of "/home/u63936157/overwatch.sas7bdat".
Your work gets saved: tables written with a libref (data ma505.clean;) are real files that survive sign-out. Tables with no libref go to work, which is deleted.
One place to change: if the folder moves, edit one LIBNAME line, not every PROC.
Organization: separate librefs for separate projects, or for raw vs. cleaned data.
One line to restore: just the LIBNAME at the top of your program, or nothing at all with an autoexec.

2.10 Keeping a library: the autoexec file
The autoexec file is a SAS program that runs automatically every time you start SAS Studio. Put your LIBNAME statement there and the library is ready every time you log in.

In SAS Studio, click More application options (top right) → Edit Autoexec File.
Add your LIBNAME statement (example below).
Click Run and check the log for errors.
Click Save. Sign out and back in to see MA505 waiting in the Libraries pane.


/* autoexec.sas: runs automatically each time SAS Studio starts */
libname ma505 "~";

Reading the output

Skewness (1.25) tells us if the data is lopsided. 0 means symmetric. A positive value means a long tail to the right (a few really high values), and a negative value means a long tail to the left. Anything past ±1 is pretty skewed, so highway MPG is skewed right. Notice the mean (26.84) is a bit higher than the median (26).
Kurtosis (6.05) tells us how heavy the tails are compared to a normal bell curve (normal = 0). A positive value means more extreme values than we’d expect, so a 6 means we probably have some outliers.
Tests for Location (Mu0=0) test whether the center of the data is 0. Student’s t tests the mean (t = mean ÷ std error = 96.7). Sign and Signed Rank test the median and don’t assume the data is normal. All the p-values are below .0001, so we reject that the average MPG is 0, which we already knew! To test something useful, change the value with mu0=: proc univariate data=sashelp.cars mu0=25; tests whether the average is different from 25.

text:
7.3 How does the DATA step process?

  CompilationChecks for syntax errorsIdentifies the column attributesEstablishes the table metadata
  
  ExecutionReads and writes dataPerforms data calculations and manipulations


During execution, the DATA step:

Reads a row from the input table
Processes each statement
Writes the row to the output table
Loops back to the top of the DATA step to read the next row from the input table


During execution, the DATA step is a loop. It reads one row, runs it through each statement from top to bottom, writes it to the output table, and goes back to the top for the next row, until the input table runs out. The spot where each row gets built is called the PDV.
crumbs: 7  Inside the DATA Step: the PDV

title: 7  Inside the DATA Step: the PDV
text:
7.4 SAS statements


Declarative: used in compilation

LENGTH, FORMAT, LABEL, DROP, KEEP
Give information to SAS, and only take effect during compilation
Can be placed in any order




Executable: used in execution

BMI = Weight / (Height**2) * 703;
Anything that tells SAS to do or change something
Order matters!









TipCheck yourself: statement order





What happens if we write Score_Avg = Score_Sum / 2; and then Score_Sum = FoodQuality + Service;?
Score_Avg will be missing. When SAS runs the first line, Score_Sum hasn’t been computed yet for that row, so it’s missing, and missing divided by 2 is missing. The order of executable statements matters.



There is one exception to “declarative statements can go anywhere”: LENGTH. It has to come before the column is first used, because SAS sets a column’s length the first time it sees it. Otherwise values can get cut off.
crumbs: 7  Inside the DATA Step: the PDV

title: 7  Inside the DATA Step: the PDV
text:
7.5 Compilation
During compilation, SAS:

checks for syntax errors
creates the program data vector (PDV)
sets up the processing in the PDV
creates the descriptor (the column information) of the output table


The PDV is an area of memory created in compilation. SAS builds one row at a time in the PDV.
It always starts with two temporary columns, _N_ and _ERROR_.

Think of the PDV as a one-row spreadsheet with a slot for every column. SAS reads a row into it, runs our statements (which fill in or change the slots), copies the finished row to the output table, and then uses the same slots for the next row. There is only ever one row in the PDV at a time.
_N_ and _ERROR_ are called temporary because they only exist in the PDV. They are never written to the output table.

7.6 Compilation: building the PDV
SAS adds the columns from the input table, then any new columns we create.

data food_survey;    set ma505.food_surv_wide;    Score_Sum = FoodQuality + Service;    Score_Avg = mean(FoodQuality, Service);run;

D means the column is dropped (not written to the output table). K means it is kept. _N_ counts the iterations, and _ERROR_ is 1 when there is a data error.

SAS knows the columns from the input table and their attributes from the table’s descriptor, without reading any data yet.
A dropped (D) column is still in the PDV, so we can still use it in calculations. It just isn’t written out at the end. That’s why DROP and KEEP don’t stop us from using a column inside the step.






TipCheck yourself: which columns end up in the output table?





Student, Restaurant, FoodQuality, Service, Score_Sum, and Score_Avg. Six columns, everything marked K. No _N_ and no _ERROR_.

title: 7  Inside the DATA Step: the PDV
text:
7.7 Execution
During execution, SAS:

initializes the PDV (new columns are set to missing)
reads a row from the input table into the PDV
processes the statements in order, and updates the PDV values
at the end of the step, writes the contents of the PDV to the output table
returns to the top of the DATA step


Execution only starts if there are no syntax errors!

If compilation finds a syntax error, like a missing semicolon, SAS stops there. No rows are read and no table is created. That’s why the log says the output table was not created, or has 0 observations.

7.13 The RETAIN statement
Recall: at the start of each iteration, new columns are set back to missing.
So what if we want a column Total that is the running total of Score?

If we create Total as a new column, it resets to missing on every row, so it can’t add up. Instead we use:
RETAIN column <initial-value>;
RETAIN leaves the value as it is in the PDV from one row to the next.

RETAIN is a declarative statement, like LENGTH and FORMAT, so it can technically go anywhere in the step. Putting it near the top, right after SET, makes our intent clear.

8.16 _ERROR_
In SAS, _ERROR_ is set to 1 when certain data or processing problems happen in a DATA step. For example:



data conversion errors
division by zero
invalid math (like the log of a negative number)
invalid array references



uninitialized columns in expressions
invalid date or time values
errors in user-defined functions or formats




What happens when _ERROR_ = 1?

a note or warning is written in the log
the value is set to missing
SAS keeps going with the next row
